title: Tax filing deadline
brief: A national tax site lets 30 million people file online. Most wait until deadline day, and traffic climbs all evening to a final-hour rush. People upload forms, check what they owe and pay. A mistake in a payment or a leak of tax data is a national story.

clarify.a: The deadline is 23:30 on the last day. Traffic builds from the afternoon and peaks in the final hour at about three times the already high evening level.

clarify.q: Can a payment be taken twice?
clarify.a: Never. Every payment must happen exactly once, even when the person presses pay again or their phone retries.

clarify.q: What if the identity-check provider rate-limits us?
clarify.a: It happens in the rush. Sign-ins that cannot be verified right now must wait, not fail forever.

clarify.q: What does an auditor ask for?
clarify.a: Proof of an audit trail, encryption, isolated personal data, backups, signed-in access and retention for years.

notes: The deadline-day curve climbs to 1.0 at 23:30, and an extra rush on top triples the last stretch.
A "write" is saving a draft or submitting a return.

Scored data retention: at least 2555 days on active authoritative stores. Copies used only for search or reports can be rebuilt. Local device history and rollup policies still require the separate protocol check.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

hints: The load arrives slowly and then all at once. What element adds servers as the day builds, and why will it still be late?
Anything that can wait should: uploads, notices and receipts go through a queue and workers, so the front stays fast.
External success must be accounted for independently of the user session. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Three things matter. Absorb a very big climb with autoscaling and a cache for what is the same for everyone. Keep slow work off the live path with queues. And prove safety: exactly-once payments and a full compliance set.

designs.name: Autoscaled front, queued back, once-only payments
designs.why: A CDN carries forms and static pages, a WAF and rate limiter keep abuse out, and an autoscaled container cluster does the live work. A distributed cache and a sharded SQL database hold the returns. Uploads, notices and receipts go via queues to workers. Payments go through an idempotency store to the processor.

tradeoffs: Autoscaling takes a few minutes to add servers, so the design pre-sizes to 20 and scales on a climb that starts hours early. A sudden minute-long jump would still hurt.
The queue lets the site accept a return in a moment and finish processing it later; the person sees "received" and gets a confirmation after.
Idempotency keys cost about $300 a month here and turn "press pay twice" from a double charge into a no-op.
The compliance set (vault, key service, audit, backups) is a fixed price of a few thousand dollars; skipping it is cheaper until the audit.
editorial.realWorld: National filing sites commonly take a large share of their season's returns in the last two or three days (approx.). Identity-check and payment partners are the usual limits in the final hour, and many agencies pre-scale and rehearse load for it.

correctness.prompt: The payment provider times out after accepting a charge. What idempotency key and payment state transitions would make a second tap safe?
correctness.discussion: Use a stable key for the logical payment, not a new key for each attempt, and bind it to the payer, amount and currency. Enforce uniqueness and store pending, succeeded and failed states durably. A timeout leaves the outcome unknown, so reconcile with the provider using the same key rather than start a fresh charge. Apply callbacks conditionally so a late failure cannot overwrite success. Record the order update and its outbox event together; a cache lookup followed by a charge leaves a race. Filing acceptance and external payment are different facts. A timeout is an unknown external outcome, not a rejection. External success must be accounted for independently of the user session.

fields.label: Step 1. A filing reaches the cutoff with payment still pending. What is recorded?
options: A durable filing id and accepted_at with separate payment status under the stated rule
fields.explanation: Filing acceptance and external payment are different facts.

fields.label: Step 2. The payment times out and the taxpayer retries. What key is used?
options: A fresh charge key per attempt
The same payment obligation key and reconciliation
fields.explanation: A timeout is an unknown external outcome, not a rejection.

fields.label: Step 3. A late callback succeeds after the page closed. What happens?
options: Conditionally settle the obligation and retain an audit receipt
Discard it because the browser session expired
fields.explanation: External success must be accounted for independently of the user session.

correctness.responsibility: Issue durable filing receipts and reconcile payments independently of deadline retries.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.
